Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verses 1–5:

﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book﴾ The servant (ʿabd) here is the Prophet (ﷺ). Describing him with servitude is an honour for him and an announcement of his special closeness. The Book is the Qur'an. ﴿And not made therein any crookedness﴾ Iwaj, with a kasra on the ʿayn, refers to meanings that are not good; with a fatha, it refers to physical objects such as a staff and the like. Its meaning is lack of straightness. It has been said here that the meaning is: there is no contradiction in it and no defect. It has also been said: He did not make it created. The wording is more general than all of that. ﴿Straight﴾ means upright. It has been said: a guardian over creation by the command of Allah, the Exalted. It has also been said: a guardian over the other books by confirming them. Its position is as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from "the Book," and its governing element is "sent down." Al-Zamakhshari rejected this, because it separates the circumstantial (ḥāl) from the one it describes (dhū al-ḥāl), and he chose that the governing element is a hidden verb whose estimated form is "made it straight." ﴿To warn of severe punishment﴾ It is connected either to "sent down" or to "straight." Its agent is the pronoun referring to the Book or to the Prophet (ﷺ). Ba's means punishment. The second object, which is "the people," is omitted, just as the other object is omitted in His saying "and warn those who," because the meaning indicates what is omitted. ﴿From Him﴾ That is, from His own presence, and the pronoun refers to Allah, the Exalted. ﴿A good reward﴾ meaning Paradise. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ That is, remaining. Its position is as a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in "for them." ﴿And to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ They are the Christians, for their saying about Jesus; the Jews, for their saying about ʿUzayr; and some Arabs, for their saying about the angels. ﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾ The pronoun refers to their saying, or to the son.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verses 7–8:

﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it﴾, meaning: that which is suitable for adornment, such as clothing and food, trees and rivers, and other things. ﴿That We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾, i.e., that We may test them as to which of them is most detached from the adornment of this world. ﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it a barren, dry earth﴾. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verses 10–12:

﴿When the youths sought refuge in the cave﴾. We will mention of their story, in brief, only what is indispensable, since people have said a great deal about it while much of what they transmitted lacks soundness. They were a people of faith, and the king of their land was a disbeliever who would kill every believer. So they fled with their religion and entered the cave to worship God therein and to hide from the king and his people. The king ordered that they be pursued. Those who pursued them reached the cave and found them, and they informed the king of this. He came to them with his soldiers and ordered that they be entered upon. The men feared to do so and said to him: "Leave them to die of hunger and thirst." God had cast a heavy sleep upon them, and they remained in that state for a long period. Then God awakened them, and they thought that they had slept a day or part of a day. So they sent one of them to buy food for them with silver coins they had with them. The seller was astonished at the coins and said: "These coins are from the time of so-and-so the king, in ancient times. Where did you get them?" The matter spread among the people. The man said: "I and my companions went out only yesterday, and we took refuge in the cave." He said: "These are the youths who departed in ancient times." They went to them and found them dead.

As for the location of their cave, it is said that it is near Palestine. Others said: it is the cave in al-Andalus, near Lushsha on the side of Granada, and in it are dead bodies and with them a dog. Ibn 'Atiyya has mentioned this and said: he entered upon them, saw them, and there was a mosque over them, and near them a building called al-Raqim, of which some walls remain. It is narrated that the king in their time was named Daqyus, and in that region are the ruins of a city called the city of Daqyus. And God knows best.

What makes this unlikely is that it is narrated that Mu'awiya passed by them and wished to enter upon them, yet Mu'awiya never entered al-Andalus. Also, the dead bodies in the cave of Lushsha are seen by people, and none of them has been struck by the terror that God mentioned concerning the People of the Cave.

﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave﴾: a metaphor for casting sleep upon them. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that We placed a barrier over their ears, then the object was omitted. ﴿For a number of years﴾: i.e., many years. ﴿Then We awakened them﴾: i.e., We roused them from their sleep. ﴿That We might know which of the two parties was best at computing the period they had remained﴾: i.e., that We might know with a knowledge that manifests in existence, since God had already known that. "The two parties" refers to those who differed concerning the duration of their stay: one party was the People of the Cave, and the other party was the people in whose time God raised up the People of the Cave. It was also said that both parties were the People of the Cave, since some of them had said: "We have stayed a day or part of a day," and others said: "Your Lord knows best how long you have stayed." ﴿Ahsa﴾ is a past-tense verb, and ﴿amadan﴾ is its object. It was also said: ﴿ahsa﴾ is a comparative noun and ﴿amadan﴾ is a specification, but this is weak, because the comparative form of the afʿal type cannot be derived from a quadriliteral verb except in rare usage.

﴿Wa-idhi i'tazaltumūhum﴾ (And when you withdraw from them): a address from some of them to others, when they resolved to flee with their religion. ﴿Wa-mā ya'budūna﴾ (and what they worship) is a conjunction with the object in i'tazaltumūhum: i.e., you left them and you left what they worship. ﴿Illā Allāh﴾ (except God): i.e., what they worship besides God. Here illā carries the meaning of ghayr (other than). This is an exceptive (muttaṣil) construction if their people worshipped God and also worshipped others alongside Him, and a disjunctive (munqaṭi') one if they did not worship God. In Ibn Mas'ud's codex it reads: "wa-mā ya'budūna min dūni Allāh" (and what they worship besides God). ﴿Fa-'wū ila al-kahf﴾ (then take refuge in the cave): this verb is the governing element of idh in i'tazaltumūhum. The meaning is that some of them said to others: "When we part from the disbelievers, let us make the cave our shelter, and rely upon God, for He will show us mercy and be gentle with us." ﴿Mirfaqan﴾ (a provision/means of comfort), with the mīm vowelled either with a fatḥa or a kasra: that by which one derives benefit and profit.

﴿And you would see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it sets, passing them on the left﴾. It is said that there is an omitted statement here, and its implied meaning is: the people sought refuge in the cave and remained there, and God struck their ears (so that they would not hear). The meaning of *tazawaru* is "inclines and turns away." The meaning of *taqridhuhum* is "cuts them off," that is, it keeps away from them, and this has the sense of cutting off. *Dhat al-yamin wa al-shimal* means "its direction," that is, to the right and to the left. The meaning of the verse is that the sun does not strike them at its rising or at its setting, so that they would not be burned by its heat. It is said that this was a *karamah* (a miracle granted to a righteous person) for them and a *kharq ʿadah* (a breach of the customary order of nature). It is also said that the entrance of the cave faced north, toward *Banat Naʿsh* (the stars of the Great Bear), and for this reason the sun did not reach them. The first view is more evident, because of His words: ﴿That is among the signs of God﴾. ﴿And they were in a spacious area of it﴾, that is, in a wide place, and this would have been open to the sun's reaching them; yet God kept it away from them. ﴿That is among the signs of God﴾: the reference is to the sun being kept from them if it is a *kharq ʿadah*; and if it is because their entrance faced north, then the reference is to their whole situation as a unit.

﴿And you would think them awake while they were asleep﴾. *Ayqaẓan* is the plural of *yaqiẓ*, meaning the one who is alert. Their eyes were open while they were sleeping, so whoever saw them would think they were awake. In His words *ayqaẓan* and *ruqud* there is *tibaq* (antithesis), and it is one of the tools of eloquent expression.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 19–20:

﴿And thus We roused them, that they might question one another.﴾ That is, just as We put them to sleep, so too We roused them, so that some of them would ask others. The lam in liyatasa'alu is the lam of result (lam al-sayrura), meaning the outcome that follows, not the purpose intended.

﴿One of them said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained."﴾ This is the statement of someone among them who sensed that the period of their sleep had been long, so he rejected the claim of those who said "a day or part of a day," but he did not know its exact length, so he attributed knowledge of it to Allah.

﴿So send one of you with this silver coin of yours﴾ al-Warq means silver. It was the dirhams they had taken as provision when they left for the cave. From this it is derived that taking provision for a traveler is better than leaving it, and from the sending of one of them it is derived that agency (wakala) is permissible. If it is asked: how is the sending of one of them connected to the remembrance of the length of their stay?

The answer is that they had said: "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained," and there is no way for you to know that. So turn to what is more important than this and more beneficial for you: send one of you ﴿to the city﴾. It was said that it is Tarsus. ﴿Let him see which food is purest﴾. It was said: most abundant; it was also said: most lawful; and it was said that he intended to buy raisins, and it was also said dates. ﴿And let him be discreet﴾ in concealing himself and in his cunning. ﴿For if they gain power over you, they will stone you﴾. That is: if they gain the upper hand over you, they will kill you by stoning. It was also said the meaning is they would stone you with words, but the first is more evident.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 21:

﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾, meaning: just as We put them to sleep and raised them up, We made the people aware of them. ﴿That they might know﴾: the pronoun refers to the people whom God made aware of the People of the Cave. That is, We made them aware of their condition, namely their waking from the long sleep, so that they might thereby take it as proof of the truth of resurrection from the graves. ﴿When they disputed among themselves about their affair﴾: the governing element of "when" (idh) is "We caused them to be found," or it is an implied verb whose estimated form is "remember." The disputants are the people who had disagreed about what to do concerning the People of the Cave, or who disagreed over whether they were dead or alive. It was also said that they disputed whether it is the bodies or the spirits, together with the bodies, that will be gathered; so God showed them the condition of the People of the Cave so that they would know that bodies are gathered. ﴿So they said: "Build over them a building."﴾ That is, over the entrance of their cave, either to obliterate their traces, or to protect them and keep away anyone who wishes to seize them or to take their dust for blessing; or so that it would be a marker for their cave, by which it would be recognized.

﴿Those who prevailed in their affair said﴾: it was said that this means the rulers; and it was said that it means the Muslims, because they had more right to them than the disbelievers, so they built over the entrance of the cave a mosque for the worship of God.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 22:

﴿They will say﴾: the pronoun refers to those who lived in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) from among the Jews or others who spoke about the People of the Cave. ﴿Guessing at the unseen﴾: that is, conjecture. It is a metaphorical use of rajm, meaning throwing. ﴿Seven, and their eighth is their dog﴾: Some people said that the waw here is the waw al-thamaniyya (the "waw of eight"), because it appears here, in His saying ﴿seven nights and eight days﴾, in His saying about the people of Paradise ﴿and its gates will be opened﴾ [39:73], and in His saying in Bara'a ﴿and those who forbid wrongdoing﴾ [9:112]. The Basrans said: the waw of eight is not established. The waw here is like the saying: "Zayd came, with a sword in his hand."

Al-Zamakhshari said: its benefit is emphasis, and it indicates that those who said "seven, and their eighth is their dog" were correct and told the truth, unlike those who said "three, and their fourth is their dog," and those who said "five, and their sixth is their dog." Ibn Atiyya said: the waw entered at the end of the report about their number to indicate that this is the final thing that was said, and if it were dropped the sentence would still be sound. Similarly, the sin (sa) entered in the first ﴿They will say﴾, and did not enter in the second and third, being dispensed with because it entered the first. ﴿Only a few know them﴾: that is, only a few people know their number, and they are from among the People of the Book. Ibn Abbas said: "I am one of that few, and they were seven, and their eighth was their dog," because He said about the three and the five ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾, and did not say that about ﴿seven, and their eighth is their dog﴾.

﴿So do not dispute concerning them except with an outward dispute﴾: lā tumari is from al-mira', which means argument, opposition and reasoning. The meaning is: do not dispute with the People of the Book concerning the number of the People of the Cave except with an outward dispute, that is, one that does not go deep into it, without exaggeration and without harshness in refuting them. ﴿And do not seek a ruling about them from any of them﴾: that is, do not ask any of the People of the Book about the People of the Cave, because God has revealed to you concerning them what suffices you from asking.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 23:

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed I will do that tomorrow," * Except [when adding], "If Allah wills."﴾ Its occasion was that the Quraysh asked the Jews about the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said to them: "Ask him about the youths who went forth in the earliest times, the People of the Cave, and about a man who reached the easts and the wests of the earth, Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the Spirit. If he answers you concerning the two and remains silent about the Spirit, then he is a prophet." So they asked him, and he said, "Tomorrow I will inform you," and he did not say, "If Allah wills." So Allah withheld revelation from him for fifteen days, and the disbelievers of Quraysh were troubled by it and spoke about it, and that grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then Jibril came with Surah al-Kahf and recounted to him in it the story of the People of the Cave and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and Allah revealed this verse as a discipline and instruction for him. He commanded him to make the exception, by the will of Allah, in every matter he intends to do in the future. His saying "tomorrow" intends the time to come, not specifically the day after his day. In the speech there is an omission required by the meaning, and its estimate is: "And never say of anything, 'Indeed I will do that tomorrow,' except that you say, 'If Allah wills,' or you say, 'Except that Allah wills,'" and the meaning is that the matter be attached to the will of Allah, His power and His strength, while he himself disclaims any power or strength. It was also said: His saying "except that Allah wills" is connected to His saying "never say." The meaning is: do not say that statement except that Allah wills that you say it, by permitting you to do so; so the will here refers to the saying, not to the act, and its meaning is the permissibility of the saying through His permission concerning it. Al-Zamakhshari related this, and Ibn Atiyya related it too, and said that it is so corrupt that the proper course was not to relate it.

ومن كتاب التسهيل لابن جزي على سورة الكهف، الآية 24:

﴿وَٱذْكُر رَّبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ﴾. قال ابن عباس: الإشارة بذلك إلى الاستثناء، أي استثن بعد مدة إذا نسيت الاستثناء أولاً، وذلك على مذهبه، فإن الاستثناء في اليمين ينفع بعد سنة. وأما مذهب مالك والشافعي فإنه لا ينفع إلا إن كان متصلاً باليمين. وقيل معنى الآية: اذكر ربك إذا غضبت. وقيل: اذكر إذا نسيت شيئاً ليذكرك ما نسيت. والظاهر أن المعنى: اذكر ربك إذا نسيت ذكره، أي ارجع إلى الذكر إذا غفلت عنه، واذكره في كل حال. ولذلك قالت عائشة رضي الله عنها: كان رسول الله ﷺ يذكر الله على كل أحيانه.

﴿وَقُلْ عَسَىٰ أَن يَهْدِيَنِ رَبِّي لأَقْرَبَ مِنْ هَـٰذَا رَشَداً﴾. هذا كلام أمر النبي ﷺ أن يقوله، والإشارة بهذا إلى خبر أصحاب الكهف، أي عسى الله أن يؤتيني من الآيات والحجج ما هو أعظم في الدلالة على نبوّتي من خبر أصحاب الكهف. اللفظ يقتضي أن المعنى: يعني أن يوقفني الله تعالى من العلوم والأعمال الصالحات لما هو أرشد من خبر أصحاب أهل الكهف وأقرب إلى الله. وقيل: إن الإشارة بهذا إلى المنسي، أي إذا نسيت شيئاً فقل: عسى أن يهديني الله إلى شيء آخر هو أرشد من المنسيّ.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verses 25–27:

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first is that it is a report about the People of the Book, as is indicated by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and they said, they remained in their cave." It is coordinated with "they will say" (sayaqulun) three (verse 22). His words ﴿Say: Allah is most knowing of how long they remained﴾ are a rejection of them concerning this number that is reported from them. The second opinion is that it is a statement of Allah, the Exalted, and that it is an explanation of what was stated in summary in His words: "So We struck upon their ears in the cave for years, a counted number" (verse 11). The meaning of His words "Say: Allah is most knowing of how long they remained" according to this view is that He is most knowing of those about whom people differed, and He has informed of the duration of their stay; so His information is the truth, because He is more knowing than people. His words "Say: Allah is most knowing" serve as an argument for the correctness of that information. "Years" (sinin) is in the accusative either as a substitute (badal) for "three hundred," or as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan), or as a specification (tamyiz). This is according to the reading with tanwin on "three hundred." It was also read without tanwin, as an annexation (idafa), and the plural was placed in the position of the singular.

﴿See how clearly He sees and hears﴾: meaning, how much He sees and how much He hears, because Allah perceives hidden things as He perceives manifest ones.

﴿They have no protector other than Him﴾: the pronoun refers either to all creation or to the contemporaries of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And He does not share His command with anyone﴾: this is a declarative statement in the reading of one who reads it with the yā' and the nominative case (raf'). It was also read with the tā' and the jussive (jazm), as a prohibition.

﴿None can alter His words﴾: it may be that by "words" here the Qur'an is meant, so the meaning is that no one alters or changes the Qur'an. It may also be that by "words" is meant the decree and the destiny (al-qadaʾ wa'l-qadar).

﴿Refuge﴾: meaning a place of shelter to which one inclines.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 18, verse 28:**

﴿And keep yourself patient﴾, that is, restrain yourself patiently, ﴿with those who call upon their Lord﴾. They are the poor among the Muslims, such as Bilal, Khabbab, and Suhayb. The disbelievers had said to him: "Drive these away, and we will sit with you." So the verse was revealed. ﴿In the morning and the evening﴾. It was said: the intended meaning is the five daily prayers. It was also said: it means supplication in general.

﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾, that is, do not go past them to the people of worldly life. Al-Zamakhshari said: one says ʿadāhu (عداه) when one passes beyond something, so this verb is transitive without a preposition. Here it was made transitive with ʿan (عن) because it includes the meaning of nabat ʿaynuhu ʿan al-rajul (نبت عينه عن الرجل), meaning that one's eye turns away from a man in contempt.

﴿Desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾: this is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), so it is connected to what precedes it. It carries the sense of giving the reason for the forbidden act mentioned in "and let not your eyes pass beyond them", meaning: do not turn away from them because of your desire for the adornment of this world.

﴿Whose heart We have made heedless﴾, that is, We made it heedless, or We found it heedless. It was said: it refers to ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn al-Fazārī, but the more apparent view is that it is general and unrestricted.

﴿Excess﴾: from tafrīṭ (التفريط), meaning neglect and waste, or from ifrāṭ (الإفراط), meaning extravagance and excess.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 29:

﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord."﴾ That is, this is the truth. ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.﴾ Its wording is a command and a giving of choice, but its meaning is that the truth has become manifest, so let each person choose for himself: either the truth that saves him, or the falsehood that destroys him. Within this is a warning (tahdid). ﴿Its enclosure⁠—﴾ As-Suradiq (the enclosure) in the language means that which surrounds a thing, such as a wall or a barrier. As for the enclosure of Hell, it has been said: it is a wall of fire, and it has been said: it is smoke. ﴿Like molten brass⁠—﴾ Al-Muhl is the sediment of oil when its heat has reached its end; this is related from the Prophet (ﷺ). It has also been said: it is whatever is melted of lead and the like. ﴿And it is an evil resting place⁠—﴾ That is, a thing by which one is supported (yartafiqu bihi); it is from ar-rifq (kindness, support). It has also been said: one reclines upon it, so it is from al-irtifaq in the sense of reclining.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 31:

﴿Those, for them﴾ is the predicate of inna (indeed), and "innā lā nuḍīʿu" (indeed, We do not waste) is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ). It is also permissible that both be predicates, or that "innā lā nuḍīʿu" be the predicate, with "ulāʾika" (those) being a resumption (istiʾnāf). The generality in His saying "man aḥsana maqāman" (whoever is best in deed) is sustained by the pronoun that links (al-ḍamīr al-rābiṭ), or one may estimate it as "man aḥsana ʿamalan minhu" (whoever is better in deed than him). It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them." ﴿Asāwir (bracelets)﴾ is the plural of ʾaswār and siwār, which is what is placed on the wrist. It was also said that asāwir is the plural of ʾaswira, and ʾaswira is the plural of siwār. ﴿Of green silk and brocade﴾: sundus is fine silk brocade, and istabraq is the thick kind of it. ﴿Al-arāʾik (couches)﴾: the beds and the furnishings.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 18, verses 32–37:**

﴿And set forth for them﴾: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers who said, "Drive away the poor among the Muslims," and to the poor whom they wanted to drive away. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 45:

﴿So the vegetation mingled﴾ The bāʾ (in bihi, "by it") is causal (bāʾ sababiyyah), and the meaning is: the plants became intermingled through it, i.e., some of them became entwined with one another because of their dense growth. ﴿Then it became dry stalks﴾ meaning crumbled and broken into pieces, and aṣbaḥa here means ṣāra (became). ﴿Which the winds scatter﴾ i.e., disperse it. The meaning of the parable is a comparison of the worldly life, in the swiftness of its passing away, to crops in their perishing after their greenness.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 46:

﴿The wealth and the children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ The verse: this is from combining two things in a single statement, and that is one of the tools of eloquent expression (adawat al-bayan). It was also read as "zeenatan" in the dual form, because it reports about two things. As for the reading of the majority, the word "zeenah" (adornment) is in the singular because it is a verbal noun (masdar).

﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾ are: "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to God), "al-Hamdu lillah" (Praise be to God), "La ilaha illa Allah" (There is no god but God), and "Allahu akbar" (God is the Greatest). This is the view of the majority, and it has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: the five daily prayers. And it was said: good deeds in general, without restriction.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 48:

﴿We shall set the mountains in motion﴾, i.e., we shall carry them (nuhammiluha). From this is His saying: "And they pass by like the passing of clouds" (Qur'an 27:88). "And after that they will become like dust scattered" (Qur'an 56:6). ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾, i.e., manifest, with the mountains removed from it. ﴿And We will gather them﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: The phrase "And We gathered them" came in the past tense after "We shall set [the mountains] in motion" only to indicate that the gathering took place before the mountains were set in motion, so that they might witness those terrors. ﴿So We will leave none of them behind﴾, i.e., We will not leave behind ﴿any one of them﴾, i.e., in rows (ṣufūf). The singular here is used in the sense of the plural. It has also been reported in a hadith: "The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows, and you [this community] make up eighty of them."

﴿Indeed, you have come to Us﴾. This is said to the disbelievers as a rebuke. ﴿Just as We created you﴾, i.e., barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised (ghurlan [ghayr mukhtatinin]).

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verses 49–50:**

﴿And the Book will be placed﴾, meaning the records of deeds. Here "the Book" is a generic noun (ism jins). ﴿He was of the jinn﴾: this is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf) that works as an explanation (ta'lil) for Iblis's refusal to prostrate. The apparent sense of this passage requires that Iblis was not one of the angels, and that his exception from them (istithna') is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), since the jinn are a category distinct from the angels. Whoever says that he was one of the angels answers this by saying that "kana" here means "sara" (became): that is, he left the category of the angels for the category of the jinn. Or [they answer] that among the angels there was a group called the jinn, who were those created from fire.

﴿So he defied the command of his Lord﴾: that is, he departed from what he had been commanded. Linguistically, fisq means going out (al-khurуj).

﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies besides Me?﴾ This is a rebuke and an admonition. The offspring of Iblis are the devils (al-shayatin), and taking them as allies means obeying them in disobeying God and disbelieving in Him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 51–54:

﴿I did not make them witness to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to their own creation﴾. The pronoun ("them") refers to the devils, in a manner that belittles them, or to the disbelievers, or to all of creation. In that case it contains a refutation of the astrologers (al-munajjimun), the people of natural temperaments (ahl al-tabaa'i'), and all other sects that speculate without knowledge (al-mutarakhrisa).

﴿Nor would I have taken the misleaders as helpers﴾: i.e., as aides (mu'in). The "misleaders" (al-mudilliyn) are those who lead the servants astray, and this strengthens the view that the intended referents are the devils.

﴿And on the day He will say, "Call upon My partners, whom you claimed"﴾: He says this to the disbelievers in a manner of reproach to them. God attributes the partners to Himself according to their claim, and He clarified this by His saying: "whom you claimed."

﴿A place of destruction (mawbiq)﴾: i.e., a place of ruin. It is either a place-name or a verbal noun from "waqaqa al-rajul," meaning the man perished. It has been said that it is a valley among the valleys of Hell. The pronoun in "between them" refers to the polytheists and their partners.

﴿And they will be certain that they are going to fall therein﴾: here the word "thann" (assumption) carries the meaning of certainty (yaqin).

﴿And they will find no place to turn away from it (masrif)﴾: i.e., no escape (mu'addal) to which they might turn.

﴿Most disputatious (jadalan)﴾: i.e., contentious argument and repelling by speech. The context of the discourse requires the censure of disputation. It is said that its cause was the dispute of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and that "man" here is intended in the generic sense.

ۚ"And what prevented the people from believing..." — the verse. Its meaning: what prevents people from faith and seeking forgiveness is that a decree be passed against them, namely that there come upon them the way of the earlier nations, which is destruction in this world, or that the punishment come upon them, meaning the punishment of the Hereafter. The word (qubulan) means "face to face," i.e., in plain sight; it is also read with two dammas (qubulan with both letters vocalized with ḍammah), and it is the plural of qabil, meaning kinds of punishment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 56–58:

﴿لِيُدْحِضُواْ﴾, i.e., "to nullify" (ليبطلوا). ﴿وَمَا أُنْذِرُواْ هُزُواً﴾, meaning the punishment. "Ma" here is either a relative pronoun (ما موصلة), with an omitted pronoun whose implied form is "they were warned of it" (أنذروه), or a verbal-noun particle (مصدرية).

﴿إِنَّا جَعَلْنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ أَكِنَّةً﴾ ("Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings"). This is either a punishment for the aversion attributed to them, or a causal explanation for it. "Akinnah" is the plural of "kinan," meaning a covering. "Waqr" means deafness. Both are used figuratively, to describe their little understanding of the Qur'an and their failure to respond to faith.

﴿فَلَنْ يَهْتَدُوۤاْ إِذاً أَبَداً﴾ ("then they will never be guided, ever"). It means those whom God has decreed will never believe.

﴿لَوْ يُؤَاخِذُهُم﴾ ("If He were to seize them"). The pronoun refers either to the disbelievers of Quraysh or to all people, based on His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ يُؤَاخِذُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلنَّاسَ﴾ ("If God were to seize the people..."), [al-Nahl: 61]. The clause is the predicate of the subject. "Al-Ghafur" (the Forgiving) and "dhu al-rahmah" (the Possessor of mercy) are two attributes that were inserted between the subject and the predicate as a preparation for what is mentioned afterward regarding the abandonment of seizure. It is possible that "al-Ghafur" is itself the predicate, and "yu'akhidhuhum" (He would seize them) is an explanation of His forgiveness and mercy. The first view is more evident.

﴿بَل لَّهُم مَّوْعِدٌ﴾ ("Rather, for them there is an appointed time"). It was said: it is death. It was said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter. It was said: it is the Day of Badr.

﴿مَوْئِلاً﴾ ("a refuge"), i.e., a place of safety. It is said: "wa'ala al-rajul" when the man sought refuge.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 59:**

﴿And those cities﴾. He means 'Ad, Thamud, and others of the earlier peoples. The intended meaning here is "the people of the cities," which is why he says, "We destroyed them." He said: 'No.' So Allah revealed to him: 'Rather, Our servant al-Khidr is more knowledgeable than you.' He said: 'O Lord, show me the way to meet him.' Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verses 77–78:

﴿So they journeyed on until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food.﴾ It is said: it was Antioch; and it is said: Barqa.

Abu Hurayrah and others said: it is in al-Andalus, and it is mentioned that it is al-Jazirah al-Khadra (Algeciras). This is according to the view that the meeting-place of the two seas is near Tangier and Ceuta. ﴿They asked its people for food﴾, i.e., they requested food from them. ﴿A wall that was about to collapse﴾, i.e., about to fall. Attributing the wanting (irada) to the wall is a metaphor (majaz), and the like of this is common in Arabic speech; its reality is that it was close to collapsing. The form of yanqaddu (ينقضّ) is yanfa'il (ينفعل); and it is said it is yaf'all with the doubled letter, like yahmarr (يحمرّ).

﴿So he set it upright﴾. It is said: he demolished it and then rebuilt it; and it is said: he wiped it with his hand and it stood upright.

﴿Had you wished, you could have taken a wage for it.﴾ That is, Musa said to al-Khidr: "Had you wished, you could have taken a wage for it," i.e., food that we might eat.

﴿He said: "This is the parting between me and you."﴾ He only said this because of his condition in his words: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me in your company﴾. Moreover, his words ﴿Had you wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾ are not a question, but they contain an implicit instruction to take a wage for it, since they were both in need of food. Here "al-bayn" (the separation/distance) is not a time-adverb; its meaning is connection and closeness. Al-Zamakhshari said: the original form is "hadha firaqu bayni wa baynika", with firaq in nunation and bayni in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf), then the verbal noun was made to be annexed to the adverb, and the demonstrative in his words "this" refers to the third question, which necessitated the parting.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verse 96–98:

﴿Until, when he had leveled [the gap] between the two cliffs﴾, i.e., between the two mountains. ﴿He said, "Blow,"﴾ meaning, blow the bellows; i.e., kindle the fire upon the iron. ﴿Molten copper﴾, i.e., melted copper; it was also said that it is lead. It is narrated that he dug the foundation until he reached water, then built the structure from blocks of iron until he filled what was between the two mountains with it, then poured molten copper over it. ﴿So they could not scale it or pierce it﴾. The original form of "isṭā'ū" is "istaṭā'ū," and the letter tā' was dropped for ease of pronunciation. The pronoun in "yaẓharūhu" refers to the barrier, and the meaning of "yaẓharūhu" is that they would climb over it and ascend its top. So the meaning is that Yajuj and Majuj are unable to climb over the barrier because of its height, nor can they breach it because of its strength. ﴿He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾. The speaker is Dhu'l-Qarnayn, and he pointed to the barrier. ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level (dakk)﴾, meaning the Resurrection; He will make it flat, leveled with the ground.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 18, verses 99–102:

﴿And We left some of them﴾ The pronoun in "taraknā" (We left) refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "Yawma'idhin" (on that day) may mean the Day of Resurrection, since it has been mentioned before; in that case the pronoun in His words "some of them" refers to all of mankind. Or it may mean "the day when the barrier is completed," and the pronoun in "some of them" refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj. The first is more preferable because of His words after it: ﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾, so that the discourse is connected. "Yamuju" (surge) is an expression for their mixing together and agitation. ﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾: the Ṣūr (Trumpet) is the horn that will be blown on the Day of Resurrection, as has come in the hadith. Isrāfīl will blow it twice: one blast for the swoon (al-ṣa'q) and the other for rising from the graves. ﴿And We will present Hell﴾, that is, We will make it manifest. ﴿Whose eyes were under a veil from My remembrance﴾ is an expression for the blindness of their insight and hearts; likewise, ﴿and they were not able to hear﴾. ﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they can take My servants as protectors instead of Me?﴾ This means that they will not have them as protectors, as is related of them that they say, "You are our protector, not them." The "servants" here are those who were worshipped besides Allah while not desiring that, such as the angels and ʿĪsā ibn Maryam. ﴿We have prepared﴾, that is, We have made ready. ﴿As a welcome (nuzul)﴾ means what is prepared for a guest and arriving visitor upon his coming. The meaning is that Hell will be in place of a welcome for them, just as the Gardens are a welcome in His words: ﴿For them the Gardens of Paradise will be a welcome (nuzul)﴾ [al-Kahf: 107]. It is also possible that "nuzul" means the place of descent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 18, verses 103–108:

﴿Say: Shall We inform you of those who are the greatest losers in their deeds?﴾ The verse refers to the disbelieving Arabs, as in the saying of God: They disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in their meeting with Him. It is also said that it refers to the monks, because they worship and think their worship benefits them, but it is not accepted from them. In His saying, "They think that they are doing good," there is a tajnis (paronomasia) of the type called tajnis al-tashif (paronomasia by variation in diacritical dots). ﴿So We shall not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning they have no good deed that can be weighed, because their deeds have been nullified. ﴿Gardens of Firdaws (Paradise)﴾: it is the highest part of Paradise, as stated in the hadith, and the word Firdaws is non-Arabic, arabicized. ﴿Desiring no change﴾, meaning no transformation or removal.
